chief_complaint: severe depressive episode with history of hypomania
hpi_details: A 35-year-old male presents to the clinic with severe depressive episode with history of hypomania. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: He thinks he completely drained his body and burned out after pushing himself way too hard during an energetic streak a few months ago.
concerns: He is worried that he will never climb out of this dark slump and will fail to support his family.
expectations: He hopes to receive medication to lift this heavy fog and a medical note to excuse him from work while he recovers.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Bipolar II depression evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Bipolar II depression is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes psychiatric assessment for an appropriate mood stabilizer or atypical antipsychotic (for example, lamotrigine or quetiapine); avoid antidepressant monotherapy and tailor treatment to individual risk factors and severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: severe depressive episode with history of hypomania

Key HPI features: A 35-year-old male presents to the clinic with severe depressive episode with history of hypomania. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Bipolar II depression.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Bipolar II depression.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Bipolar depression without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Active suicidal ideation with plan.
management_principles: Urgently assess suicide risk, including intent, plan, means, and ability to remain safe; arrange emergency psychiatric evaluation when risk is imminent.
A qualified prescriber should select and monitor an appropriate mood stabilizer or atypical antipsychotic; avoid antidepressant monotherapy.
Arrange timely psychiatric follow-up and provide safety planning and counselling.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

must_ask.say: How has your mood, sleep, and energy been recently?

history.answer: Doctor, I have been feeling overwhelmingly down and exhausted for the past month, and it keeps getting harder to get through each day.
It began about four weeks ago and has gotten steadily worse, weighing on me nearly every single day from morning until night.
The sadness and heaviness feel at their absolute worst right when I wake up in the morning, and lift only slightly by late evening.
Nothing specific happened at work or at home that would explain this; the low mood seemed to settle in out of nowhere.
I have completely lost interest in everything I used to enjoy, like playing tennis or listening to music; nothing brings me pleasure anymore.
I have trouble falling asleep and wake up around four in the morning unable to go back to sleep, getting barely four hours a night.
My appetite has dropped significantly over the past month, and my clothes feel loose since I have lost about four kilograms.
I feel completely drained of energy all day long, as though my limbs are made of lead.
My mind feels foggy, so reading a simple email takes forever and making minor decisions at work feels impossible.
I keep feeling like a failure and blaming myself for letting my team and my family down, even though my wife tells me I am being too hard on myself.
Everything I do feels physically slowed down, and speaking takes tremendous effort.
When the exhaustion peaks, fleeting thoughts cross my mind that maybe it would be easier if I did not wake up, but I do not want to end my life.
No, I have never made any plans, I do not have any means, and I have never attempted suicide.
My wife and my family mean the world to me, and knowing how much they love me keeps me anchored and seeking help today.
I have been calling in sick to work two or three days a week and have stopped answering calls from friends because I cannot face anyone.
history.topic: Impact on daily life and work

history.answer: About six months ago, I had a five-day stretch where I slept only three hours a night, felt energized, talked unusually fast, and started multiple creative projects without feeling tired.
history.topic: Periods of elevated mood and energy

history.answer: No, I never got arrested, spent recklessly, or needed to go to the hospital during that energetic week, though my friends remarked I was unusually chatty.
No, I have never heard voices or seen things that others could not, and I do not hold any unusual beliefs.
I have a beer or two maybe twice a month socially, and I do not use cannabis, sleeping pills, or any recreational drugs.
No, I have not felt unusually cold, my bowel movements are normal, and I have not had neck swelling or tremors.
I had a milder episode of depression about two years ago that lasted a couple of months and eventually cleared up on its own.
Back during that first depression two years ago, a doctor gave me an antidepressant, but after three days I felt terribly restless and agitated, so I stopped it immediately.
My maternal aunt was diagnosed with bipolar disorder, but nobody in my family has ever attempted or died by suicide.
I think I just totally burnt myself out after going a hundred miles an hour on all those projects a few months back.
I'm scared that I won't be able to shake this awful darkness and I won't be able to provide for my family.
I was hoping you could give me something to clear this heavy cloud and write a doctor's note for some time off work.
I have no history of high blood pressure, diabetes, thyroid disease, or any chronic medical illnesses.
I had an appendectomy when I was twelve years old, but I have never had any other surgeries or hospitalizations.
I am not currently taking any prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs, or herbal supplements.
I have no known allergies to medications, foods, or materials like latex.
I work as an office accountant and live in an apartment with my wife; we do not have children yet.
